data.title: Rybník – Krivín: a hillfort above the Hron at the Slovak Gate
data.excerpt: The Krivín hillfort sits on a narrow rocky tongue where the valley of the Hron contracts into an easily controlled pass at the south-eastern edge of the Slovak Gate. Six enclosures, a main rampart 520 m long and finds ranging from the Final Bronze Age to the 10th century led Štefan Janšák to rank it among the most perfect hillforts.
data.metaTitle: Rybník – Krivín: a hillfort at the Slovak Gate
data.metaDescription: The Krivín hillfort guards an easily controlled pass at the edge of the Slovak Gate, with six enclosures on a rock cliff almost 150 m above the Hron.

children.text: The “Krivín” hillfort is in many respects highly interesting, both for its position and for its shape. The valley of the Hron narrows unusually at this point, forming an easily controlled pass at the south-eastern edge of the so-called Slovenská brána (Slovak Gate). On one side the hillfort is washed by the southward-flowing Hron. The narrow mountain tongue on which the hillfort extends is the western offshoot of Bukovský vrch, spot heights 314 and 315 (316 (?) on the hiking map), and it drops away abruptly in a steep, almost vertical rock face to the river Hron. In the east the hillfort is bounded by the Hruštená (formerly Zrybacká) valley. A blue hiking trail leads to the hillfort from Tlmače. The hillfort was investigated in the 1920s by Štefan Janšák; later only sporadic investigations took place there, and in 2002 a trial excavation was carried out aimed at refining the dating and the course and condition of the fortification.

The rock on which the hillfort stands, also called Krásna skala, splits easily in a vertical direction, which made possible the formation of a monumental rock cliff that – as Janšák writes – recalls the canyons of the Colorado River in its height, appearance and beauty. For almost 150 m one wall of the hillfort rises vertically above the surface of the river Hron. From it there opens a wide view, which in itself predetermined the advantageous strategic position of the hillfort.

There are few places in Slovakia offering as much natural security combined with the immediate proximity of passable terrain and a fertile plain as Krivín does. From the north and north-west it is protected by the river Hron, difficult to ford for most of the year. A vertical rock rises straight from the water itself. To the north-east the steep rock does give way to a slope, but one steep enough to need no fortification, on which a palisade could have stood. On the western side the ridge climbs 72 m in height over a length of 110 m, thus forming a rock cliff that is almost inaccessible. Only the southern hillside of the ridge descends more gently into the Zrybacká valley, though even here with a gradient of up to 45°, which forms a considerable obstacle to ascent. From the north-east and north the hillfort is connected to Bukovský vrch by a flat ridge (which later turns at a right angle to the east). It follows from the above that there is only one comfortable ascent into the hillfort, namely along the flat ridge from the north-east.

The rampart fortification is adapted very purposefully to this natural configuration, and these two factors together create the whole hillfort, which consists of six enclosures, I to VI. Enclosure I is protected from the north-west by a steep slope and from the south-east by an artificial rampart 640 m long and about 0.5 metres high. On the north-eastern side there are no surviving defensive structures protecting this enclosure, which, given its position and the absence of any cultural remains, can be regarded only as an extensive bailey. There follows a whole system of arc-shaped ramparts, linking up with one another and creating a perfect fortress.

children.text: Rampart j-k-h (see the plan by Štefan Janšák) runs from the top of the slope above the Hron in an arc to the north-east and to the south. It runs almost horizontally, for a length of 275 m, reaching at most 1.5 m in height in places. From point k the rampart k-o-r-š branches off from it. Rampart i-j-l, 140 m long and up to 3 m high on the outer side, forms the second line of defence against forcible entry along the ridge. Rampart e-h-l-g then represents the main defence. Beginning at point g, on the rock above the Hron, it climbs through point i until it reaches point h and continues westwards, from where it climbs back again to point e. Towards the east, from where entry into the hillfort was easiest, this rampart reaches a height of up to 8 m (below spot height 320), while on the southern side, in the stretch e-h, it is in places scarcely discernible. Here, on the steep slope, it was pointless. The total length is 520 m. Rampart c-d-e-f, about 1 m high in one part and further on the slope already looking only like a low, flat terrace, has a length of 435 m. Finally rampart b-d runs southwards in a bulging arc for a length of 405 m, from spot height 245 (at point b) up to a level of 270, where it joins the preceding rampart at point d.

The material from which the ramparts are built comes directly from the hillfort, that is, clay mixed with larger and smaller fragments of basalt. The main defensive rampart contains a large quantity of sherds, which would suggest that it was repaired several times, and that on those occasions sherds of vessels already broken earlier found their way into it. Two gateways, m and n, are clearly discernible, established by the original inhabitants of the hillfort for the sake of comfortable entry. They are ordinary breaks in the ramparts, without any blocking work. These gateways still offer the relatively most comfortable access today.

As has already been mentioned, six enclosures are formed by the ramparts described above. Enclosure I, with the function of a bailey, remains open on the north-eastern side. All the others are completely enclosed, either by a steep rock face or by artificial banks. Enclosure II, with an area of 75 ares, and enclosure III, with an area of 25 ares, are, given their position and size, only defensive baileys of purely strategic significance, unlike bailey I, which certainly also had an economic significance. Only the further enclosures IV, V and VI were properly inhabited. Of these, enclosure IV in particular has every prerequisite of the necessary comfort and safety. It occupies a pear-shaped plateau whose main axis is 375 m long, the greatest width being 150 m. Its surface rises only very gently in a direction parallel to the river Hron. Protected from the north-east by three baileys I, II and III, and from the south-west in turn by two almost impregnable enclosures V and VI, enclosure IV played the role of an acropolis, to which the largest number of finds also bears witness. The surface of enclosure V has great differences in height, as a result of which it is unsuitable for habitation and permanent residence. Its significance may be strategic. Enclosure VI extends on the south-western spur of the rocky peninsula, occupying a natural plateau suitable for comfortable habitation and residence. The total area of the hillfort is about 9.7 hectares.

Janšák states that in terms of safety, comfort of habitation and also the proximity of cultivated plains that provided the earliest inhabitants with a livelihood, Krivín can be ranked among the most perfect hillforts.

During the investigation in the 1920s no remains of dwellings, refuges or cisterns were found. Only during surface investigation without digging were large fragments of a maul made of quartz found, a trachyte fragment of a disc that served either as a grinding stone or as a weapon, and further smaller, completely preserved pebbles of very regular shape (grinding stones). The usual clay fired to a red-brown colour, with impressions of straw and chaff, occurs in great abundance. The most striking traces of the former culture, however, are the large quantity of sherds 1–1.5 cm thick, heavily graphite-coated on the outer surface of the vessels, or without a graphite coating. Sherds with ornament were also found. Part of the pottery belongs to the period of the Hallstatt culture, and another part, decorated with wavy lines, testifies that the hillfort was also inhabited by our Slavic ancestors, in the course of the 9th and 10th centuries.

children.text: The trial excavation carried out at the hillfort in 2002 produced a large number of further finds, mainly pottery, and slightly corrected the course of the fortification in some parts of the hillfort. As the authors of the excavation state, the sherd material includes all the basic forms of Lusatian pottery production from
the transition between the Bronze Age and the Hallstatt period

, above all amphorae, vases and profiled cups, and numerous bowls with inturned as well as twisted rims and barrel-shaped pots are not lacking either. Similar finds have been made, for example, at Nitra-Šindolka, Pobedim, at the Ostrá hora hillfort in Kvašov and at Horné Srnie. Part of the pottery bears features of the Kalenderberg culture, which on the territory of present-day Slovakia manifested itself above all in the south-west (for example the Molpír hillfort). For an understanding of the economic hinterland of the hillfort it is important that chronologically identical remains from the Final Bronze Age to the Hallstatt period, the same as at the hillfort, have also been identified at a settlement (settlements?) lying on the opposite terrace of the Hron in the cadastral area of the local part of Psiare. Although not numerous, the pottery fragments of the Great Moravian period are nevertheless exceptionally important in view of the long-standing assumptions about Slavic occupation of Krivín. The finds mentioned from the later periods come exclusively from the areas of enclosures V and VI, and the finds from the open settlement at Psiare correspond to them in date as well. Krivín was therefore demonstrably
used as a hillfort by our Slavic ancestors as well.

It can moreover be assigned to the system of guard hillforts situated at the entrance to the Slovak Gate. Other Slavic hillforts are to be found in the immediate vicinity – Tlmače-Festunok, Starý Tekov, Malé Kozmálovce and Hronský Beňadik. It is assumed that in the 10th century these guard hillforts may have formed the frontier line of the Principality of Nitra after it had come under the sphere of Magyar power. This can be regarded as one of the signals that the Slavs living north of this frontier still maintained their independence from the emerging Kingdom of Hungary in the course of the 10th century.

children.text: The authors of the 2002 excavation state that enclosures IV–VI in particular were used at the end of the Final Bronze Age and in the first phase of the Hallstatt period to build a hillfort with a massive and progressively improved fortification system. In the construction of the circuit ramparts a box construction was used, and when their bank was consolidated, and in the most exposed stretches, it was also strengthened with a drystone wall. Already in this period the rampart enclosed at least three separate, mutually adjoining enclosures that were used for permanent and long-term occupation. Provisionally we can synchronise the occupation of Krivín at the turn of the Bronze and Iron Ages with the final phases of the hillforts at Sitno, at Zobor near Nitra and at Ostrá hora in Horné Srnie. It may also be contemporary with the other hillforts in the Tríbeč range (Žibrica, Kostoľany pod Tríbečom-Veľký Lysec, Kovarce-Veľký Tríbeč, Klátova Nová Ves-Šiance and probably with the beginnings of the occupation of the Molpír hillfort in Smolenice).
